story: A replacement draw can repeat a row. For the usual bootstrap, draw n times from n training rows: the expected unique share is one minus the chance a particular row is missed in every draw.

aha.observation: Eight draws from eight rows cover 65.64% of rows on average. The familiar 63.21% is the large-n limit, not a guarantee for every sample.

data.title: Repeats leave some rows unseen.
data.heading: Expected coverage · replacement sampling
data.prompt: why does a bootstrap sample contain only about 63% of the unique training rows?
data.instructions: Try n = 8, then increase n. Distinguish expected coverage from a single realized draw.

reference.title: Why about 63% appear
reference.caption: Worked example. Rounded limit $1/e≈0.368$ gives expected coverage $1-0.368=0.632$.

calculations: For m replacement draws from n rows: q=(n−1)/n; omission=q^m; coverage=1−q^m; expected distinct count=n*coverage.
Usual bootstrap uses m=n. At n=8: omission=(7/8)^8=0.34360891580581665; coverage=0.6563910841941833; expected rows=5.251128673553467.
For m=r*n, large-n coverage tends to 1−exp(−r); r=1 gives 0.6321205588285577. Deep r=2 or 3 deliberately changes the experiment, not the source bootstrap claim.
The source plot shows omission. This card shows its exact complement as coverage, labelled separately.
